items.name: Request
items.doc: `raw_headers` is exactly the CRLF-separated "name: value" lines this request's header block was made of, unparsed -- not a map[str]str. Building a map costs an allocation for the map plus roughly two more per header, on every request, whether or not anything ever reads a header; most requests never do. `header`/`header_or` scan this directly (strings.find_field, no allocation for the search itself); `headers()` builds a map from it on demand for a caller that genuinely wants one. Constructed only by `parse`/`read` (off the wire) or `request` (validated, from a map) -- never assign this field directly from unvalidated bytes; a value containing "\r\n" inside a hand-built block is a second header no map ever held.

items.name: WireFrame
items.doc: `read` couples two things that only sometimes belong together: filling the caller's buffer and framing what's in it. serve_conn needs the split for frame dispatch: read_frame frames with the same scans/errors/rules as read, but returns the parsed head (method/path strs, header block, body) instead of a Request -- so the router matches on strs with no raw copy, no rescan, no second slice. Offsets stay for Frame callers and tests; the serve path does not use them.

items.name: Frame
items.doc: The request WITHOUT materialising method/path/version strs: framing offsets only. `read`/`serve` use this when they only route on the raw path bytes (see path_matches below); `parse` keeps returning strs for callers that actually need them.

items.doc: header()'s two real call sites (Ctx.header in zokor, the WebSocket handshake) are both `header(...) ?? fallback` already -- this is that, without the opt allocation `??` unwraps.

items.name: headers
items.doc: Every header a request carries, as a map -- built fresh on each call by scanning raw_headers once. Nothing in either repo iterates a request's headers today (confirmed by grep), which is what makes "built on demand" the right default over a cached field: a cache nothing reads is pure cost. Walks the same line shape scan_headers does, for a different reason (that one validates and extracts two offsets; this one assumes an already-valid block and extracts every name and value) -- kept as two functions rather than one parameterized by what to do with each line, which would obscure both to save repeating six lines.

items.name: request

items.doc: Builds a Request from a map the way the eager parser builds one off the wire: a header name or value may not contain CR or LF (an application- or test-constructed header gets no such check for free the way one read off the wire does -- this is where that rule lives for this path), and a name may not contain the colon that separates it from its value on the wire. Both are a real hazard, not a theoretical one, now that raw_headers is what a request's headers actually are: a value containing "\r\n" would be concatenated straight into the block below as a SECOND header line -- injection -- if it weren't rejected first.

items.name: parse_frame

The request line is validated (two spaces, HTTP/1.x token); the header block is validated by scan_headers; the body is framed by frame(). Callers that need strs (logging, tests) use parse(); the server path matches/routes directly on these offsets -- see path_matches and method_is below -- so the ~10 framing strs per request never exist.

The old builder path stays below as serialize_builder for the differential test; this is what `serialize` and `write`'s fallback call, so an oversized response costs a few allocations instead of ~40.  The remaining handful is load-bearing, not waste: one to_bytes per fill_str piece (the str->bytes copy the compiler cannot fuse), one filtered-extra list, and the response_conn scan's own line strs. Counting them is what keeps this honest -- see the probe notes.

Allocates nothing.

items.name: read_frame
items.sig: fn read_frame(c: &mut link, buf: wire, filled: int, idle_deadline: until, header_deadline: until, body_deadline: until) -> result[WireFrame, str]
items.doc: read_frame: read's framing, plus the parsed head the router matches on. Implemented INSIDE read's loop shape (not as read-plus-copy): read compacts the buffer before returning, so after read there is no head left to copy -- buf[0..filled] is the NEXT request. This duplicates read's loop deliberately (same scans, same errors, same close rules), and the duplication is the contract: any change to read's framing must land here too.  What differs from read: on a complete frame the method/path strs and the header block + body are COPIED OUT of the wire ONCE -- the same strs + copies read already pays (hd.method/path, hd.headers, hd.body) -- and NO separate message copy is made. The old shape did to_bytes(buf[0..end]) PLUS parse_frame over the copy PLUS wants_close_scan over the copy: a full second framing pass and a whole-message copy per request. Now the WireFrame carries what the router needs directly: method/path strs for the enum + Request build, headers/body slices for the Ctx. Routing matches on strs (==), never on raw bytes -- no path_is_at rescan, no per-route to_bytes. The message copy is gone entirely.  Chunked bodies: hd.body IS the reassembled copy (one alloc the old path also spent); the WireFrame body is that copy directly. Three deadlines, not one, because "how long should this wait" has three different honest answers depending on what the connection is doing: idle_deadline while nothing has arrived at all yet (a kept- alive connection between requests, or a fresh one that never sends anything -- this is the one that should be generous, since a real client legitimately sits idle between requests); header_deadline once bytes have started arriving but the request line and headers aren't complete yet; body_deadline once the headers are in but a declared body hasn't fully arrived. header_deadline and body_deadline are both the tight, slow-loris-shaped ones -- a client that has started a request and then trickles it in a byte at a time is not the same risk as one that hasn't sent anything yet, and idle_deadline being long must not become an amplifier for that. Recomputed fresh every loop iteration rather than tracked as a separate flag: frame_head_wire's own re-parse of the same (only ever growing) buffer already answers "is the header complete yet" idempotently, so re-deriving which phase this recv is in from that costs nothing extra and can't drift out of sync with it.

items.name: StaticBody
items.doc: serialize()'s GC allocations (~40 of them for a typical response, see serialize()'s own comment) replaced with two passes over the caller's own arena: size, then fill. If the response is larger than what's left of the arena, falls back to serialize() + send_bytes rather than letting a.wire(need) past capacity kill the task -- a slow response stays a slow response instead of becoming a dropped connection.  Responses with exactly the `text_response` shape (one content-type, nothing else) take the fixed fast path above: no map iteration, no integer str, no intermediate bytes. Anything else uses the general `emit` below, unchanged. A static route's answer: status, content type, and body -- no Response struct, no extra list, nothing to shape-check. serve_conn gets one from serve_static and hands it straight to write_static, which sends the PREBUILT keep-alive rendering (assembled once at registration -- see static_render below) with one wire alloc and one memcpy. The static snapshot lives on the Route (see router.sl); this is just the per-request view of it.

items.name: write_static
items.sig: fn write_static(c: &mut link, b: StaticBody, a: &mut arena, close: bool, deadline: until) -> result[int, fault]
items.doc: The static emit: the keep-alive rendering is prebuilt, not emitted. Hot path (HTTP/1.1 keep-alive, which is every wrk/ab request): one wire, one memcpy, one send -- no probe pass, no Response struct, no map, no integer str, no per-piece puts. The close variant (HTTP/1.0, Connection: close) is rare and pays the emit cost below; it never touches the hot path.

A rendering is shared by every request, so the date cannot be part of it; a renderer outside this package (zokor's, with its security headers) ends its header block with this line to get the same. Any other rendering is sent as it is.

items.name: client_read_response
items.sig: fn client_read_response(cn: Conn, r: Reader, t: Transport, wch: chan[WMsg], stream: int, timeout_ns: int, max_body: int) -> result[Response, str]
items.doc: Read frames until `stream`'s response is complete. For a connection carrying one stream at a time; use client_start/client_call for more. `timeout_ns` bounds the whole response, and `max_body` its DATA.

items.name: client_start
items.sig: fn client_start(t: Transport, lim: Limits) -> result[Client, str]
items.doc: Handshake on `t` and start the connection's writer and reader tasks. From here the Client owns `t`: its reader closes it, once, after both tasks have stopped (client_close waits for that). If the handshake fails, the writer has stopped before this returns and the caller still owns `t`.

items.name: client_call
items.sig: fn client_call(c: Client, method: str, scheme: str, authority: str, path: str, headers: [Header], body: bytes, timeout_ns: int, max_body: int) -> result[Response, str]
items.doc: One request/response exchange on `c`, safe to call from many tasks at once. Waits for a free stream slot first. `timeout_ns` bounds the exchange from the moment its HEADERS are queued; `max_body` bounds the response DATA. Never retried: a transport error can arrive after the server acted, and only the caller knows whether that is safe to repeat.

items.name: client_close
items.doc: Stop taking calls, send GOAWAY and close the connection; calls in flight fail with "closed by the client". Returns once the connection is fully closed -- its reader and writer stopped and the transport closed -- so the fd number is free for reuse only then. Closing the fd while the reader was still parked on it let a new connection reuse the number under a waiter that was not its own, and that connection's reads stopped waking. Safe to call more than once, and after the connection failed on its own.

items.name: W_RAW
items.sig: let W_RAW = 0; // pre-built frames, not flow controlled
items.doc: ---- writer messages -------------------------------------------------  Everything the writer task needs arrives on ONE channel, tagged.  When this was written slang had no `select`, so a writer watching both "here is a response" and "the peer granted more window" on two channels could only ever block on one of them. `select` exists now and would compile -- but the single tagged stream is still the better design here, and stays. Two channels would make the ORDER between a grant and a body a race the writer has to reason about; one channel makes it the order they were sent, for free, and leaves the writer an ordinary state machine with a single blocking point.

items.doc: Build a response. The body is handed over UNFRAMED: the writer owns the peer's window and its max frame size, so it -- not the handler -- decides how the body is cut into DATA frames and when each may go.  Like HTTP/1.1's writer: a date unless the handler set one (RFC 9110 6.6.1), and for 1xx, 204 and 304 -- which have no content -- neither content-length nor body.

No content-length: with trailers the message is delimited by END_STREAM, and gRPC peers do not expect one. Trailers may not carry pseudo-headers (RFC 9113 §8.1), and each block must fit one frame at the smallest maximum a peer may advertise, since this layer does not split header blocks.

items.name: Limits
items.doc: ---- deadlines -------------------------------------------------------  Four separate budgets, in nanoseconds, because they defend against four different peers and want wildly different numbers.  `idle` is the generous one on purpose: an HTTP/2 connection sitting open with no streams is completely normal -- that is the whole point of connection reuse -- so timing it out aggressively breaks correct clients. `request` is the strict one: once a client has started a request it must finish it, and dribbling DATA forever is exactly the slowloris shape.

items.name: is_timeout
items.doc: The reserved error string net.recv_until / net.send_until return when a deadline passes. Exposed as a predicate so callers can react to a slow peer (GOAWAY with ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM) differently from a broken one, without hardcoding the text.

items.name: MAX_HEADER_FIELDS
items.doc: Our own limits, advertised in SETTINGS and enforced on receipt.

items.name: RESET_BURST
items.doc: ---- Rapid Reset (CVE-2023-44487) ------------------------------------  A peer opens a stream and immediately RST_STREAMs it. From its side the stream is closed the instant it opens, so a concurrency limit never sees it -- while the server has already done the HPACK decode and, in most designs, started the work. Repeat and the server is driven at whatever rate the attacker can write frames.  Cancelling a request IS legitimate: a browser navigating away resets its in-flight streams, and a client that gives up on a slow endpoint should. So a flat "no resets" rule would break correct clients. What is not legitimate is resetting nearly everything you open, forever.  Hence a burst plus a ratio: RESET_BURST cancellations are free, and after that a peer whose resets outnumber half of what it opened is ending the connection. A browser that abandons a page load trips neither; a Rapid Reset flood resets every stream it opens, so it trips both the moment the burst is spent.

items.name: our_settings
items.doc: Our SETTINGS: a modest frame size, and push disabled because server push is deprecated and no current client wants it.

items.name: gate
items.doc: ---- the stream gate -------------------------------------------------  The connection layer cannot cap concurrency on its own: it does not spawn the handlers, the CALLER does. (slang has function values now, so handing it a callback would compile -- but that only moves the same question inside, and the answer would still be this.) So the bound lives in a token channel the caller holds, and this is the mechanism plus the vocabulary for it.  A gate is a chan[bool] holding `n` tokens. gate_enter takes one and blocks when none are left; gate_leave puts one back. That blocking IS the backpressure -- the reader stops pulling frames while every slot is busy, which is the correct answer to "more work than I can do", and far better than the alternative measured before this existed: 3002 concurrent handler tasks from a peer we had told our limit was 100.  It also solves shutdown. Closing the writer channel while handlers are still in flight panics them with "send on closed channel", and nothing else could tell whether any were left. gate_drain waits for every token to come home, so the close is safe by construction.  The one rule: gate_leave must run on EVERY path out of a handler, including error returns. A lost token permanently shrinks the connection's capacity, and losing all of them wedges that connection (only that one -- the failure is bounded and visible, not a crash).

items.name: gate_drain
items.doc: Wait until every handler has finished, by collecting all `n` tokens. Call before chan_close on the writer channel.

items.name: Transport
items.doc: ---- transport -------------------------------------------------------  h2 runs over cleartext TCP (h2c, prior knowledge) or over TLS, and the two are reached through different runtime calls: net.recv_until on an fd, net.tls_recv_until on an SSL handle. Everything above this point is identical either way, so the difference is confined to one struct and two functions rather than duplicated through the whole layer.  This matters beyond tidiness: browsers speak HTTP/2 ONLY over TLS with ALPN, so a connection layer that can only do fds cannot serve a browser at all, however conformant the rest of it is.

items.name: transport_tls

items.name: alpn_is_h2
items.doc: RFC 7301 §3.1: the peer either selected "h2" or it did not. A server that advertised h2 and http/1.1 must look, because a browser offered both and may well have picked http/1.1 -- feeding an HTTP/1.1 client into this layer produces "bad connection preface", which is true but unhelpful.

items.name: read_frame
items.sig: fn read_frame(r: Reader, t: Transport, max_frame: int, u: until) -> result[Frame, str]
items.doc: Pull bytes until at least one complete frame is buffered, then return it and keep the remainder. Note the `&mut *c` at every site below that forwards this borrow: passing `c` directly MOVES it, so the second call would fail with "use of moved value". Reborrowing keeps the caller's borrow usable.  `u` bounds the WHOLE call, not each recv: a peer that sends one octet every second must still finish the frame inside the budget, which is what makes this a slowloris defence rather than a keepalive check. Pass until_never() only where blocking forever is genuinely intended.

Before it the connection is idle and gets the generous `idle` budget, refreshed by each control frame that arrives -- a client PINGing a kept-alive connection is behaving correctly and must not be disconnected. After it the strict `request` budget applies to the request as a WHOLE and is never refreshed, so no amount of dribbled DATA or CONTINUATION can extend it.

Returning str here would be a silent data-loss bug: symbol 0 is NUL, and to_str truncates there, so a value containing \x00 came back empty. Header field values are byte sequences on the wire; the caller decides whether to reject NUL (read_string does) rather than having the codec quietly drop everything after it.  Padding rules (RFC 7541 §5.2) are enforced rather than ignored: the tail must be fewer than 8 bits, must be all ones, and must not encode a symbol. A decoder that skips these accepts streams a conforming one rejects, which is how HPACK implementations end up disagreeing.

items.doc: The nearest float (rounding the top 64 bits; huge values give infinity).

items.name: Int.format
items.sig: fn format(self: Int, base: int) -> str
items.doc: The digits in `base` (2 to 36, lowercase letters), with a leading '-' when negative.

items.name: Int.bytes_be
items.doc: |self| as big-endian bytes, no leading zero byte (empty for 0).

items.name: rat
items.sig: fn rat(n: Int, d: Int) -> opt[Rat]
items.doc: n / d, reduced; none for a zero denominator.

items.name: rat_parse
items.doc: A fraction from "3/4", "-7", "0.125" or "-2.5e-3" (exact: 0.1 is 1/10, not the float nearest it). Exponents are limited to +-10000.

items.name: Rat.denominator
items.doc: Always positive.

items.name: Rat.add
items.sig: fn add(self: Rat, o: Rat) -> Rat

items.name: Rat.sub

items.name: Rat.mul

items.name: Rat.div
items.sig: fn div(self: Rat, o: Rat) -> opt[Rat]
items.doc: none when dividing by zero.

items.name: Rat.cmp
items.sig: fn cmp(self: Rat, o: Rat) -> int

items.name: Rat.eq
items.sig: fn eq(self: Rat, o: Rat) -> bool

items.name: Rat.floor
items.doc: The largest Int at or below the fraction.

items.name: Rat.ceil
items.doc: The smallest Int at or above it.

items.name: Rat.round
items.doc: The nearest Int, halves to even.

items.name: Rat.float_of
items.doc: The nearest float (num and den each rounded once: within a few ulps; exact for fractions whose parts fit 53 bits).

items.name: Rat.format
items.doc: "n/d", or "n" for a whole number.

items.name: Rat.format_decimal
items.sig: fn format_decimal(self: Rat, places: int) -> str
items.doc: The decimal expansion to `places` digits after the point, rounded half to even.

items.name: npv
items.doc: Net present value at `rate` per period of flows[0] now, flows[1] one period later, and so on. Horner's rule: one division per flow.

items.name: irr
items.doc: The internal rate of return: the rate at which npv(rate, flows) is 0. Safeguarded Newton on the exact derivative inside a bracket found by scanning from -0.99 upward, so it converges whenever a root exists in (-0.99, 1000). An error when the flows never change sign (no rate can balance them) or no root lies in that range. Flows that change sign more than once can have several rates; this returns the lowest.

items.name: xnpv
items.sig: fn xnpv(rate: float, flows: [float], days: [int]) -> float
items.doc: npv for flows on given days: flows[i] lands days[i] days after day 0, discounted at the annual `rate` over actual/365 years (the XNPV convention). days need not be sorted.

items.name: xirr
items.doc: The annual rate at which xnpv is 0 (XIRR).

items.name: pmt
items.sig: fn pmt(rate: float, nper: int, pv: float, fv: float, at_start: bool) -> float
items.doc: The payment per period that repays present value pv (and leaves future value fv) over nper periods at rate per period: the PMT of a spreadsheet. at_start is true for payments at the start of each period (an annuity due). pmt(0.05/12, 360, 250000, 0, false) is -1342.05.

items.name: fv
items.sig: fn fv(rate: float, nper: int, pmt: float, pv: float, at_start: bool) -> float
items.doc: The future value after nper periods of payment pmt from present value pv: the FV of a spreadsheet.

items.name: pv
items.sig: fn pv(rate: float, nper: int, pmt: float, fv: float, at_start: bool) -> float
items.doc: The present value of nper payments of pmt and a final fv: the PV of a spreadsheet.

items.name: nper
items.sig: fn nper(rate: float, pmt: float, pv: float, fv: float, at_start: bool) -> float
items.doc: The number of periods for payments of pmt to take pv to fv: the NPER of a spreadsheet (fractional). NaN when they never can.

items.name: ipmt
items.sig: fn ipmt(rate: float, period: int, nper: int, pv: float, fv: float, at_start: bool) -> float
items.doc: The interest part of payment number `period` (1-based): IPMT.

items.name: ppmt
items.sig: fn ppmt(rate: float, period: int, nper: int, pv: float, fv: float, at_start: bool) -> float
items.doc: The principal part of payment number `period`: PPMT.

items.name: effective_rate
items.sig: fn effective_rate(nominal: float, n: int) -> float
items.doc: The annual effective rate of a nominal rate compounded n times a year.

items.name: nominal_rate
items.sig: fn nominal_rate(effective: float, n: int) -> float
items.doc: The nominal rate, compounded n times a year, with annual effective rate `effective`.

items.name: compound
items.sig: fn compound(principal: float, rate: float, years: float, n: int) -> float
items.doc: principal grown at the annual `rate` for `years`, compounded n times a year (n <= 0: continuously).

items.name: cagr
items.sig: fn cagr(start: float, end: float, years: float) -> float
items.doc: The compound annual growth rate taking `start` to `end` over `years`.

items.name: Payment
items.doc: One line of an amortisation schedule.

items.name: amortize
items.sig: fn amortize(principal: decimal.Decimal, annual_rate: decimal.Decimal, periods: int, per_year: int) -> result[[Payment], str]
items.doc: The schedule repaying `principal` at `annual_rate` (0.05 for 5%) in `periods` equal payments, `per_year` a year, at the principal's scale. Interest each period is the balance times annual_rate / per_year, rounded half-even to the cent; the payment is the level payment rounded the same way, and the last payment is adjusted so the balance ends at exactly zero. Every line adds up: payment = interest + principal, and the principals sum to the loan.

items.name: prorate
items.sig: fn prorate(amount: decimal.Decimal, weights: [decimal.Decimal]) -> result[[decimal.Decimal], str]
items.doc: `amount` split in proportion to decimal weights (shares, hours, usage), adding up to `amount` exactly at its scale, by largest remainder as decimal.allocate does for int weights.

items.name: apply_bps
items.sig: fn apply_bps(amount: decimal.Decimal, bps: decimal.Decimal, mode: decimal.Rounding) -> opt[decimal.Decimal]
items.doc: amount * bps / 10000, rounded to amount's scale: a fee or spread in basis points. none on overflow.

items.name: bps_change
items.sig: fn bps_change(a: float, b: float) -> float
items.doc: The change from a to b in basis points: 10000 * (b - a) / a.

items.name: progressive
items.sig: fn progressive(amount: decimal.Decimal, bounds: [decimal.Decimal], rates: [decimal.Decimal], scale: int, mode: decimal.Rounding) -> result[decimal.Decimal, str]
items.doc: A marginal (progressive) charge: the part of `amount` in each bracket is charged at that bracket's rate, like income tax or tiered card fees. `bounds` are the ascending upper edges of every bracket but the last; `rates` has one more entry than `bounds`. progressive(1500, [1000], [0.02, 0.01]) is 1000 * 0.02 + 500 * 0.01 = 25. Rounded once, at the end, to `scale`.

items.name: tiered
items.sig: fn tiered(amount: decimal.Decimal, bounds: [decimal.Decimal], rates: [decimal.Decimal], scale: int, mode: decimal.Rounding) -> result[decimal.Decimal, str]
items.doc: A volume-tier charge: the whole amount at the rate of the tier it falls in (bounds as in progressive: the tier is the first bound at or above amount, else the last). Rounded to `scale`.

items.name: vwap
items.doc: The volume-weighted average price. NaN when the volumes sum to 0.

items.name: vwap_decimal
items.sig: fn vwap_decimal(prices: [decimal.Decimal], volumes: [decimal.Decimal], scale: int, mode: decimal.Rounding) -> result[decimal.Decimal, str]
items.doc: VWAP in decimals, exact until the final division at `scale`.

items.name: twap
items.sig: fn twap(prices: [float], times: [int], end: int) -> float
items.doc: The time-weighted average price over [times[0], end]: each price holds from its time until the next one (or end). times ascend. NaN when the span is empty.

items.name: Candle
items.doc: One bar of open, high, low, close and volume for [start, start + width).

items.name: candles
items.sig: fn candles(times: [int], prices: [float], volumes: [float], width: int) -> [Candle]
items.doc: Trades (times ascending, in any unit) rolled into candles of `width`, aligned to multiples of width; intervals without trades are skipped.

items.name: CandleBuilder
items.doc: Builds candles from a live trade feed, one trade at a time.

items.name: candle_builder
items.doc: A builder of candles `width` wide (at least 1).

items.name: CandleBuilder.add
items.sig: fn add(self: CandleBuilder, t: int, price: float, volume: float) -> opt[Candle]
items.doc: Adds a trade; returns the previous candle when this trade starts a new interval. A trade earlier than the current candle is counted in it (late prints are not dropped).

items.name: CandleBuilder.flush
items.doc: The candle in progress, if any, ending it.

items.name: max_drawdown
items.doc: The largest fall from a running peak, as a fraction of the peak (0.25 for a 25% drawdown). 0 for fewer than two prices or a series that only rises.

items.name: EARTH_RADIUS
items.doc: The mean Earth radius (IUGG), metres.

items.name: point
items.sig: fn point(lat: float, lon: float) -> Point
items.doc: A point; latitude in [-90, 90], longitude wrapped into [-180, 180).

items.name: distance
items.sig: fn distance(a: Point, b: Point) -> float
items.doc: The great-circle distance in metres (haversine): accurate for any pair of points, antipodes included, on the spherical Earth.

items.name: distance_exact
items.sig: fn distance_exact(a: Point, b: Point) -> opt[float]
items.doc: The distance in metres on the WGS-84 ellipsoid (Vincenty's inverse formula, 1975). none for nearly antipodal points, where the iteration does not converge; use distance() there.

items.name: bearing
items.sig: fn bearing(a: Point, b: Point) -> float
items.doc: The initial bearing from a toward b, degrees clockwise from north in [0, 360). Along a great circle the bearing changes as you go.

items.name: destination
items.sig: fn destination(from: Point, bearing_deg: float, meters: float) -> Point
items.doc: The point `meters` from `from` along the initial bearing (spherical).

items.name: midpoint
items.sig: fn midpoint(a: Point, b: Point) -> Point
items.doc: The midpoint of the great-circle path between a and b.

items.name: Box
items.doc: A latitude/longitude rectangle. When it crosses the antimeridian, min_lon > max_lon: a longitude is inside when it is >= min_lon OR <= max_lon.

items.name: bounding_box
items.sig: fn bounding_box(center: Point, meters: float) -> Box
items.doc: The smallest box holding every point within `meters` of center (spherical; Chan's method). Query an index with the box, then keep the rows whose distance() is within the radius. A box around a pole spans every longitude.

items.name: in_box
items.sig: fn in_box(b: Box, p: Point) -> bool
items.doc: Whether p is inside the box (edges included), across the antimeridian too.

items.name: geohash
items.sig: fn geohash(p: Point, chars: int) -> str
items.doc: The geohash of p with `chars` characters (1 to 12; 7 is about 150 m, 9 about 5 m): nearby points share prefixes, so it indexes well as a string key.

items.name: geohash_box
items.doc: The cell a geohash names. An error for an empty hash, one longer than 12 or a character outside the geohash alphabet (either case).

items.name: geohash_decode
items.doc: The centre of a geohash's cell.

items.name: geohash_neighbors
items.doc: The eight cells around a geohash, at its length: N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW. A radius search covers the cell and its neighbours. Cells beyond a pole are left out.

items.name: contains
items.doc: Whether p lies inside the polygon given by its vertices (in order, either direction, closed or not), by the even-odd rule in plain latitude/longitude: right for geofences that are small next to a hemisphere and do not cross the antimeridian or a pole.

items.name: area
items.doc: The area of a polygon in square metres on the spherical Earth (the spherical-excess formula of Chamberlain and Duquette), for polygons not crossing the antimeridian.

items.name: distance_to_segment
items.sig: fn distance_to_segment(p: Point, a: Point, b: Point) -> float
items.doc: The shortest distance in metres from p to the great-circle segment a-b (spherical): the cross-track distance when the foot of the perpendicular falls between a and b, else the nearer endpoint. For "is the courier within 50 m of the route".

items.name: empty
items.doc: A curve with no points, for `??` defaults: every value is NaN.

items.name: linear
items.doc: Straight lines between the points.

items.name: step
items.doc: A staircase: the value of the last point at or below x (the tier a quantity falls in). Before the first point: its value under Clamp, NaN under None.

items.name: monotone
items.doc: A monotone cubic (Fritsch and Carlson 1980, with Fritsch-Butland slopes): smooth, through every point, and never rising above or dipping below its neighbours, so a monotone table stays monotone. The safe choice for rates and prices.

items.name: spline
items.doc: The natural cubic spline: the smoothest curve through the points (a continuous second derivative, zero at the ends). It can overshoot between points; use monotone when that matters.

items.name: Curve.at
items.sig: fn at(self: Curve, x: float) -> float
items.doc: The value at x.

items.name: Curve.at_all
items.doc: The values at each of xs, in one pass when xs ascend.

items.name: Curve.slope
items.sig: fn slope(self: Curve, x: float) -> float
items.doc: The derivative at x (0 on a step curve, and outside the knots under Clamp).

items.name: Curve.set_extrapolate
items.sig: fn set_extrapolate(self: Curve, mode: Extrapolate) -> Curve

items.name: Curve.copy
items.doc: A curve over the same knots with its own lookup memory, for another task.

items.name: Grid
items.doc: A table of values over a rectangular grid, read by bilinear interpolation: prices by (weight, distance), rates by (term, amount).

items.name: grid
items.sig: fn grid(xs: [float], ys: [float], values: [float]) -> result[Grid, str]
items.doc: A grid over ascending xs and ys with len(xs) * len(ys) values, row by row. Outside the grid the nearest edge value is used.

items.name: Grid.at
items.sig: fn at(self: Grid, x: float, y: float) -> float

items.name: mod_pow
items.sig: fn mod_pow(b: int, e: int, m: int) -> int
items.doc: b^e mod m, by squaring: O(log e). 0 when m <= 0 or e < 0 (a negative power needs mod_inv first); 1 mod m for e = 0.

items.name: mod_mul
items.sig: fn mod_mul(a: int, b: int, m: int) -> int
items.doc: (a * b) mod m, in [0, m), without overflow; 0 when m <= 0.

items.name: ext_gcd
items.sig: fn ext_gcd(a: int, b: int) -> Bezout
items.doc: The extended Euclidean algorithm: g = gcd(a, b) and x, y with a * x + b * y = g.

items.name: mod_inv
items.sig: fn mod_inv(a: int, m: int) -> opt[int]
items.doc: The x in [0, m) with a * x = 1 (mod m); none when a and m share a factor (no inverse exists) or m <= 0.

items.name: is_prime
items.doc: Whether n is prime: exact for every int (deterministic Miller-Rabin with the seven bases Jim Sinclair found to cover all of 64 bits), after trial division by the small primes. false for n < 2.

items.name: next_prime
items.doc: The smallest prime >= n (2 for n <= 2); none past the largest int prime.

items.name: prev_prime
items.doc: The largest prime <= n; none for n < 2.

items.name: primes_below
items.doc: Every prime below n, ascending: the sieve of Eratosthenes over the odd numbers, n / 2 bytes of memory. Empty for n <= 2.

items.name: factorize
items.doc: The prime factorization of |n|, ascending by prime: 360 is [{2, 3}, {3, 2}, {5, 1}]. Empty for 0, 1 and -1. Trial division by the small primes, then Pollard's rho (Brent's variant) on what is left, with is_prime deciding each part: fast for any int whose second-largest prime factor is below about 10^12.

items.name: divisors
items.doc: Every positive divisor of |n|, ascending; empty for 0.

items.name: totient
items.doc: Euler's totient: how many integers in [1, n] share no factor with n. 0 for n <= 0.

items.name: crt
items.doc: The Chinese remainder theorem: the x in [0, lcm(moduli)) with x = residues[i] (mod moduli[i]) for every i. The moduli need not be coprime; none when the congruences contradict each other, a modulus is <= 0, the lists differ in length, or the lcm overflows an int.

items.name: binomial_mod
items.sig: fn binomial_mod(n: int, k: int, p: int) -> int
items.doc: n choose k modulo a prime p (Lucas's theorem), for n and k too large to compute the coefficient itself; 0 for k outside [0, n]. p must be prime (it is not checked: a composite p gives a wrong answer, not an error).

items.name: fibonacci
items.doc: The n-th Fibonacci number (F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1) by fast doubling; none for n < 0 or past F(92), the last that fits an int.

items.name: Root
items.doc: A root: f(x) is (near) zero. fx is f at x; evals counts calls to f.

items.name: Min
items.doc: A minimum of f on an interval: f(x) = fx.

items.name: Integral
items.doc: An integral, with an estimate of its absolute error.

items.name: Bracket
items.doc: A bracket [lo, hi] with f(lo) and f(hi) of opposite signs (or one 0).

items.name: no_root
items.doc: NaNs, for `??` defaults: (r ?? optimize.no_root()).x is NaN on error.

items.name: bracket
items.sig: fn bracket(f: fn(float) -> float, lo: float, hi: float) -> result[Bracket, str]
items.doc: Widens [lo, hi] geometrically (by 1.6 each side, up to 50 times) until f changes sign across it.

items.name: bracket_with
items.sig: fn bracket_with[C](f: fn(float, C) -> float, ctx: C, lo: float, hi: float) -> result[Bracket, str]

items.name: bisect
items.sig: fn bisect(f: fn(float) -> float, lo: float, hi: float, tol: float) -> result[Root, str]
items.doc: Bisection: halves [lo, hi] until it is within tol. Slow (one bit per step) but certain; prefer brent.

items.name: bisect_with
items.sig: fn bisect_with[C](f: fn(float, C) -> float, ctx: C, lo: float, hi: float, tol: float) -> result[Root, str]

items.name: brent
items.sig: fn brent(f: fn(float) -> float, lo: float, hi: float, tol: float) -> result[Root, str]
items.doc: Brent's method (Brent 1973, the zeroin of netlib): inverse quadratic interpolation and secant steps, falling back to bisection whenever they would not shrink the bracket fast enough. Superlinear on smooth f, never slower than bisection. The default root finder.

items.name: brent_with
items.sig: fn brent_with[C](f: fn(float, C) -> float, ctx: C, lo: float, hi: float, tol: float) -> result[Root, str]

items.name: newton
items.sig: fn newton(f: fn(float) -> float, df: fn(float) -> float, x0: float, tol: float) -> result[Root, str]
items.doc: Newton's method from x0 with derivative df: quadratic convergence near a simple root, but it can diverge from a poor start. Use newton_safe when a bracket is known.

items.name: newton_with
items.sig: fn newton_with[C, D](f: fn(float, C) -> float, df: fn(float, D) -> float, ctx: C, x0: float, tol: float, dctx: D) -> result[Root, str]
items.doc: newton with data: f and df each take ctx. (The derivative's own data is passed as dctx, so f and df can differ in what they need.)

items.name: newton_safe
items.sig: fn newton_safe(f: fn(float) -> float, df: fn(float) -> float, lo: float, hi: float, tol: float) -> result[Root, str]
items.doc: Safeguarded Newton (rtsafe): Newton steps that stay inside a bracket [lo, hi] where f changes sign, with bisection whenever a step would leave it or shrink it too slowly. Fast and certain.

items.name: newton_safe_with
items.sig: fn newton_safe_with[C, D](f: fn(float, C) -> float, df: fn(float, D) -> float, ctx: C, lo: float, hi: float, tol: float, dctx: D) -> result[Root, str]

items.name: golden
items.sig: fn golden(f: fn(float) -> float, a: float, b: float, tol: float) -> result[Min, str]
items.doc: Golden-section search for the minimum of a unimodal f on [a, b]: the interval shrinks by 0.618 per evaluation. Needs no derivative and no smoothness; prefer brent_min for smooth f.

items.name: golden_with
items.sig: fn golden_with[C](f: fn(float, C) -> float, ctx: C, a: float, b: float, tol: float) -> result[Min, str]

items.name: brent_min
items.sig: fn brent_min(f: fn(float) -> float, a: float, b: float, tol: float) -> result[Min, str]
items.doc: Brent's minimisation (Brent 1973, localmin; scipy's fminbound): parabolic interpolation through the best three points, golden-section steps when a parabola is not trustworthy. On [a, b], for unimodal f.

items.name: brent_min_with
items.sig: fn brent_min_with[C](f: fn(float, C) -> float, ctx: C, a0: float, b0: float, tol: float) -> result[Min, str]

items.name: simpson
items.sig: fn simpson(f: fn(float) -> float, a: float, b: float, tol: float) -> result[Integral, str]
items.doc: Adaptive Simpson's rule: splits wherever the two halves disagree with the whole by more than tol (absolute), with Richardson's correction. For smooth f on a finite interval.

items.name: simpson_with
items.sig: fn simpson_with[C](f: fn(float, C) -> float, ctx: C, a: float, b: float, tol: float) -> result[Integral, str]

items.name: integrate
items.sig: fn integrate(f: fn(float) -> float, a: float, b: float, abs_tol: float, rel_tol: float) -> result[Integral, str]
items.doc: Adaptive Gauss-Kronrod (7-point Gauss, 15-point Kronrod, as QUADPACK's QAG): the interval with the largest error estimate is halved until the total error is within max(abs_tol, rel_tol * |integral|). Infinite bounds are mapped onto a finite interval (x = t / (1 - t^2) and its one-sided forms). The general-purpose integrator.

items.name: integrate_with
items.sig: fn integrate_with[C](f: fn(float, C) -> float, ctx: C, a: float, b: float, abs_tol: float, rel_tol: float) -> result[Integral, str]

items.name: hash_str
items.doc: A 64-bit hash of a str: strings.hash widened and remixed.

items.name: hash_int
items.doc: A 64-bit hash of an int.

items.name: jump
items.sig: fn jump(key: u64, buckets: int) -> int
items.doc: The bucket in [0, buckets) for a 64-bit key (Lamping and Veach 2014): each bucket gets 1/buckets of the keys, and going from n to n+1 buckets moves only the 1/(n+1) that the new bucket takes. O(log n), no memory. buckets below 1 count as 1.

items.name: jump_str
items.sig: fn jump_str(s: str, buckets: int) -> int
items.doc: jump() of a str key.

items.name: jump_int
items.sig: fn jump_int(x: int, buckets: int) -> int
items.doc: jump() of an int key.

items.name: Rendezvous
items.doc: Rendezvous hashing (Thaler and Ravishankar 1996): each node scores the key, and the highest score wins. A node leaving moves only its own keys, spread evenly over the rest. Weighted scores follow Schindelhauer and Schomaker: -weight / ln(u) for u the node's hash of the key in (0, 1), which gives each node keys in proportion to its weight.

items.name: rendezvous
items.doc: Nodes of equal weight. Their order does not matter to the mapping; pick() returns an index into this list.

items.name: rendezvous_weighted
items.doc: Nodes with weights (a weight at or below 0, or NaN, means the node gets nothing). A missing weight counts as 1.

items.name: Rendezvous.pick
items.sig: fn pick(self: Rendezvous, key: u64) -> opt[int]
items.doc: The index of the node for this key hash; none when there are no nodes (or every weight is 0).

items.name: Rendezvous.pick_n
items.sig: fn pick_n(self: Rendezvous, key: u64, n: int) -> [int]
items.doc: The indexes of the n highest-scoring nodes, best first: the primary and then its replicas, each a different node. Fewer when there are fewer nodes.

items.name: Rendezvous.pick_str
items.sig: fn pick_str(self: Rendezvous, key: str) -> opt[int]

items.name: Rendezvous.pick_int
items.sig: fn pick_int(self: Rendezvous, key: int) -> opt[int]

items.name: Rendezvous.pick_n_str
items.sig: fn pick_n_str(self: Rendezvous, key: str, n: int) -> [int]

items.name: Rendezvous.node
items.sig: fn node(self: Rendezvous, i: int) -> str
items.doc: The name of node i (as given).

items.name: Ring
items.doc: A consistent-hash ring (Karger et al. 1997) with virtual nodes: each node puts `points * weight` markers on a 64-bit circle, and a key belongs to the first marker clockwise from its hash. Adding or removing a node moves only the keys next to its markers.

items.name: ring
items.doc: An empty ring putting `points_per_weight` markers per unit of weight (100 to 200 keeps the share of each node within a few percent).

items.name: Ring.add
items.sig: fn add(self: Ring, name: str, weight: int) -> bool
items.doc: Adds a node (or changes its weight, 1 to 1000). False for an empty name.

items.name: Ring.remove
items.sig: fn remove(self: Ring, name: str) -> bool
items.doc: Removes a node; its keys move to the next markers. False when it was not on the ring.

items.name: Ring.get
items.sig: fn get(self: Ring, key: u64) -> opt[str]
items.doc: The node for this key hash; none on an empty ring.

items.name: Bloom
items.doc: "Have I seen this key?" in about 10 bits per key at 1% false positives, never a false negative. The split-block layout (Putze et al. 2007, as Parquet and Impala use it): each key sets one bit in each of the eight 32-bit words of a single 256-bit block, so an add or a lookup touches one cache line instead of seven scattered ones. Use it in front of a database or a cache to skip lookups that would miss, or to remember idempotency keys cheaply.

items.doc: A filter sized for `n` keys at a false-positive rate of `fpp`: the bits Parquet's formula gives, -8n / ln(1 - fpp^(1/8)), in whole blocks. n is at least 1; fpp is clamped to [1e-6, 0.5]. bloom(1000000, 0.01) is 1.2 MB. Past `n` keys the rate climbs: size for the peak.

items.doc: How often each key occurred, in fixed memory (Cormode and Muthukrishnan 2005): `depth` rows of `width` counters, each key adding to one counter per row and reading the smallest. An estimate is never below the true count, and with probability 1 - delta is at most epsilon * total above it. For rate limiting, abuse detection, and finding heavy keys among millions without a map entry each.

items.name: Cuckoo
items.doc: A set membership filter that can also delete (Fan et al. 2014): each key keeps a 16-bit fingerprint in one of two buckets of four slots. Unlike a Bloom filter it can remove a key, so it fits sets that change: active sessions, in-flight job ids, revoked tokens.  Remove only keys that were added: removing a key that never was can evict a different key sharing its fingerprint.

items.name: Histogram
items.doc: Latency (or any non-negative int) percentiles in fixed memory, to a stated relative precision, merging exactly: the log-linear bucketing of HdrHistogram. Values below 2^precision are counted exactly; above that, each power of two is split into 2^(precision-1) equal buckets, so a reported quantile is within 2^-precision of the true one (precision 7: 0.8%). histogram(60000000, 7) covers 1 us to 60 s in 1,344 counters, 10.5 KB, however many values are recorded.  let h = sketch.histogram(60000000, 7); h.record(elapsed_us); h.quantile(0.99); h.mean(); h.max(); h.buckets([1000, 5000, 25000, 100000]);   // Prometheus le= counts

items.name: Reservoir
items.doc: A uniform random sample of k items from a stream of unknown length, in O(k) memory: every item seen so far is in the sample with the same probability. Algorithm L (Li 1994) skips ahead between replacements, so most items cost a counter increment and no random draw.  The sample is your own list, of any type: offer() says where the current item goes.  let keep: [Event] = []; let rs = sketch.reservoir(100, rand.new(7)); for e in events { if let slot = rs.offer() { if slot == len(keep) { push(keep, e); } else { keep[slot] = e; } } }

items.name: TopK
items.doc: The k heaviest keys of a stream in O(k) memory (Space-Saving, Metwally et al. 2005): every key whose true count is above total / k is in the list. A key not being tracked replaces the one with the smallest count and inherits that count as its possible error. O(log k) per add.  Each key lives in a fixed slot; the min-heap orders slot numbers, so a heap swap moves two ints and the key map is touched once or twice per add, never per swap.

Feed outcomes one at a time and stop as soon as it decides; on average it needs far fewer observations than a fixed-size test with the same error rates (alpha: deciding p1 when it is p0; beta: deciding p0 when it is p1). Peeking is part of the design, so stopping early does not inflate the error rate.

items.name: sprt
items.sig: fn sprt(p0: float, p1: float, alpha: float, beta: float) -> Sprt
items.doc: A test of p0 against p1 (both in (0, 1), different) with error rates alpha and beta (in (0, 1)); invalid input decides nothing ever.

items.name: Sprt.add
items.sig: fn add(self: Sprt, success: bool) -> Decision
items.doc: One observation. Once decided, further observations change nothing.

items.name: Sprt.add_n
items.sig: fn add_n(self: Sprt, successes: int, n: int) -> Decision
items.doc: A batch: successes of n.

items.name: Sprt.count
items.doc: Observations taken.

items.name: Sprt.log_ratio
items.doc: The log-likelihood ratio so far: positive leans to p1.

items.name: sum
items.doc: The sum of xs, compensated: the exact rounding error of each addition (Knuth's TwoSum) is carried and added back at the end. 0 for an empty list; an infinity or NaN in xs gives the plain sum's inf or NaN.  Two independent running sums take alternate elements, so consecutive additions do not wait on each other: one chain held a sum to the latency of a float add per element, about half the speed of a plain loop. Every list function here sums the same way, in place -- they used to collect the terms in a list first and sum that, which for variance on a million values made the pushes 90% of the time.  A `for x in xs` loop, not a `while` over indices: the for loop takes its safepoint once around the loop and reads elements unchecked, where a while loop brackets every iteration and bounds-checks every index -- twice the time per element.

items.name: product
items.doc: The product of xs; 1 for an empty list.

items.name: mean
items.doc: The arithmetic mean; NaN for an empty list.

items.name: weighted_mean
items.doc: The mean with weights ws (one per value); NaN when the lengths differ, the list is empty, or the weights sum to 0.

items.name: geometric_mean
items.doc: The geometric mean, exp(mean(log x)): for growth rates and ratios. 0 if any value is 0; NaN for an empty list or a negative value.

items.name: harmonic_mean
items.doc: The harmonic mean, n / sum(1/x): for averaging rates. 0 if any value is 0; NaN for an empty list or a negative value.

items.name: min
items.doc: The smallest element; none for an empty list. NaN never compares smaller, so a float list's NaNs are passed over.

items.name: max
items.doc: The largest element; none for an empty list. NaNs are passed over.

items.name: spread
items.doc: max - min, as a float; NaN for an empty list.

items.name: sorted_floats
items.doc: xs as floats, sorted ascending (NaN first, as sort.floats orders it): what median and quantile work on. Compute it once and use the _sorted variants when asking for several quantiles of one list.

items.name: median
items.doc: The middle value, or the mean of the two middle values; NaN for an empty list. Copies and sorts: O(n log n).

items.name: quantile
items.doc: The q-quantile (q in [0, 1]) by linear interpolation between the two nearest ranks -- type 7 in Hyndman and Fan, the default of R, NumPy and Excel's PERCENTILE.INC. NaN for an empty list or q outside [0, 1].

items.name: quantile_sorted
items.doc: quantile on a list already sorted ascending (sorted_floats), without copying it.

items.name: percentile
items.doc: quantile with p in percent: percentile(xs, 95) is quantile(xs, 0.95).

items.name: quartiles
items.doc: The three quartiles, by quantile's method.

items.name: iqr
items.doc: The interquartile range, q3 - q1.

items.name: mode
items.doc: The most frequent value, the smallest of them on a tie; none for an empty list. Floats compare exactly, so 0.1 + 0.2 and 0.3 are different values.

items.name: variance
items.doc: The sample variance (divided by n - 1): the variance of the population the values were drawn from, estimated without bias. NaN for fewer than two values. pvariance is the variance of exactly these values.

items.name: pvariance
items.doc: The population variance (divided by n); NaN for an empty list.

items.name: stddev
items.doc: The sample standard deviation, sqrt(variance).

items.name: pstddev
items.doc: The population standard deviation, sqrt(pvariance).

items.name: mad
items.doc: The median absolute deviation, median(|x - median(xs)|): a spread that one wild value cannot move, unlike stddev. Unscaled; multiply by 1.4826 to estimate a normal distribution's stddev.

items.name: zscores
items.doc: Each value's distance from the mean in population standard deviations (SciPy's zscore). All NaN when every value is the same.

items.name: skewness
items.doc: The skewness, the population third standardized moment (Fisher-Pearson g1): 0 for a symmetric distribution, positive with a long right tail. NaN for an empty list or when every value is the same.

items.name: kurtosis
items.doc: The excess kurtosis, m4 / m2^2 - 3: 0 for a normal distribution, positive for heavier tails. NaN for an empty list or constant values.

items.name: covariance
items.doc: The sample covariance of xs and ys (divided by n - 1); NaN when the lengths differ or there are fewer than two pairs.

items.name: correlation
items.doc: Pearson's correlation coefficient r, in [-1, 1]; NaN when the lengths differ, there are fewer than two pairs, or either list is constant.

items.name: spearman
items.doc: Spearman's rank correlation: Pearson's r of the values' ranks, so any monotonic relationship scores 1, not just a straight line. Tied values share the mean of their ranks.

items.name: ranks
items.doc: Each value's rank, 1 for the smallest; tied values share the mean of the ranks they span ([10, 20, 20, 30] ranks as [1, 2.5, 2.5, 4]).

items.name: linear_regression
items.doc: The least-squares line y = intercept + slope * x through the points. Every field is NaN when the lengths differ, there are fewer than two points, or every x is the same.

items.name: histogram
items.doc: Counts xs into `bins` equal-width bins over [min, max]; the last bin also holds max itself. NaNs are not counted. bins below 1 is taken as 1, and a list of one repeated value gets one bin of width 1 around it.

items.name: Running
items.doc: Count, mean, variance, min and max of a stream (Welford's algorithm): O(1) per value, numerically stable, no samples kept.  let r = stats.running(); r.add(12.5).add(9.0); r.mean(); r.stddev(); r.max();

items.name: ewma
items.doc: alpha in (0, 1]: 0.1 forgets slowly, 0.5 quickly. Clamped into range.

items.name: ewma_half_life

items.name: Digest
items.doc: Streaming quantiles: a merging t-digest (Dunning and Ertl, 2019). The stream is summarized as at most about `compression` weighted centroids, small near the extremes and large in the middle, so p99 and p999 stay accurate (to well under 1% of rank at the default 100) where a fixed-width histogram would need to know the range up front. Digests merge, so each worker can keep its own.  let d = stats.digest(); d.add(latency_ms); d.quantile(0.5); d.quantile(0.99);

items.name: parse_url
items.doc: postgres://user:password@host:port/database?sslmode=require  Recognised parameters: sslmode, sslrootcert, application_name, host and port. Any other parameter is an error rather than ignored: a misspelt "sslmdoe=require" that was silently dropped would connect in the clear, and nothing would ever say so.  sslmode: disable      cleartext. require      TLS, certificate and hostname verified. verify-full  the same as require (the libpq spelling of it). prefer, allow, verify-ca are refused. The first two fall back to cleartext when TLS fails, which is exactly what an attacker in the middle would arrange; verify-ca checks the chain but not the host.  With no sslmode the default is "require" -- except for a loopback host, where it is "disable", because traffic that never leaves the machine gains nothing from TLS and a local development server almost never has it configured.  A Unix-domain socket is named by its DIRECTORY, as libpq does: either percent-encoded as the host (postgres://app@%2Fvar%2Frun%2Fpostgresql/db) or as ?host=/var/run/postgresql. The socket file is <dir>/.s.PGSQL.<port>. Postgres does not use TLS over one, so sslmode defaults to disable and asking for require is an error.

items.doc: Runs SQL with no parameters through the simple protocol, which accepts several statements separated by semicolons -- a migration, a schema. Returns the rows affected by the last statement. Rows a statement returns are read and discarded.  Never build `sql` from untrusted input: use query() and parameters.

items.name: stream
items.sig: fn stream(c: Conn, sql: str, args: [Arg], deadline: until) -> result[Rows, str]

items.name: next_row
items.sig: fn next_row(c: Conn, rows: Rows, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
items.doc: Reads the next row of a stream into `rows` (at index 0). Returns false once there are no more; rows.affected and rows.tag are set then.

items.name: stream_close
items.sig: fn stream_close(c: Conn, rows: Rows, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
items.doc: Ends a stream early. The server is asked to cancel the query first -- and that request is seen through before the rest is drained, so it can never land on a LATER query on this connection -- then whatever it had already sent is read and dropped. The connection is then free.

items.name: copy_in_start
items.sig: fn copy_in_start(c: Conn, sql: str, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
items.doc: Starts COPY ... FROM STDIN. Send data with copy_in_send, then finish with copy_in_end -- or copy_in_abort, which rolls the COPY back.

items.name: copy_in_send
items.sig: fn copy_in_send(c: Conn, data: bytes, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
items.doc: Sends COPY data. It need not end on a row boundary; the server reassembles it. An error in the data is reported by copy_in_end.

items.name: copy_in_end
items.sig: fn copy_in_end(c: Conn, deadline: until) -> result[int, str]
items.doc: Ends the COPY. Returns the number of rows loaded, or the server's error about the data -- in which case nothing was loaded.

items.name: copy_in_abort
items.sig: fn copy_in_abort(c: Conn, reason: str, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
items.doc: Abandons the COPY: the server discards everything sent. Ok once the server has confirmed; its "COPY from stdin failed" is the expected answer, not an error.

items.name: copy_from
items.sig: fn copy_from(c: Conn, sql: str, data: bytes, deadline: until) -> result[int, str]
items.doc: COPY ... FROM STDIN in one call. Returns the rows loaded.  pg.copy_from(c, "COPY users (id, email) FROM STDIN (FORMAT csv)", to_bytes("1,a@example.com\n2,b@example.com\n"), dl)

items.name: copy_out_start
items.sig: fn copy_out_start(c: Conn, sql: str, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
items.doc: Starts COPY ... TO STDOUT. Read it with copy_out_next.

items.name: copy_out_next
items.sig: fn copy_out_next(c: Conn, deadline: until) -> result[opt[bytes], str]
items.doc: The next piece of COPY output -- in text and CSV formats, one row -- or none when it is complete.

items.name: copy_to
items.sig: fn copy_to(c: Conn, sql: str, deadline: until) -> result[bytes, str]
items.doc: COPY ... TO STDOUT in one call, buffered (up to the 256 MiB result limit; stream a larger one with copy_out_start / copy_out_next).

items.name: listen
items.sig: fn listen(c: Conn, channel: str, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]

items.name: unlisten
items.sig: fn unlisten(c: Conn, channel: str, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
items.doc: "*" stops listening on every channel.

items.name: notify
items.sig: fn notify(c: Conn, channel: str, payload: str, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]

items.name: wait_notification
items.sig: fn wait_notification(c: Conn, deadline: until) -> result[opt[Notification], str]
items.doc: The oldest queued notification, or waits for one until the deadline: none then. Unlike every other call, reaching the deadline here is not an error and does not break the connection -- waiting is the point.

items.name: col
items.sig: fn col(rows: Rows, name: str) -> int
items.doc: The index of the column called `name`. Panics if there is none: the query and the code reading it disagree, which is a bug, not a condition to handle.

items.name: is_null
items.sig: fn is_null(rows: Rows, r: int, c: int) -> bool

items.name: get_text
items.sig: fn get_text(rows: Rows, r: int, c: int) -> str
items.doc: Any column, in Postgres's text form: numbers, dates, uuid and json all arrive this way.

items.name: timestamp_rfc3339
items.sig: fn timestamp_rfc3339(cell: str, has_tz: bool) -> opt[str]
items.doc: int2, int4, int8 and oid. A timestamptz or timestamp cell as RFC 3339 text: Postgres writes "2026-10-13 09:30:15.123456+00" (a space, and an hour-only offset when the minutes are zero); this is "2026-10-13T09:30:15.123456+00:00". A timestamp without a time zone names no instant and is read as UTC, as Go's drivers read it. none for infinity, -infinity and BC dates, which a timez.Time cannot hold, and for text that is not a Postgres timestamp.

items.name: get_time
items.sig: fn get_time(rows: Rows, r: int, c: int) -> result[timez.Time, str]
items.doc: The instant in a timestamptz (or timestamp, read as UTC) cell. err for another column type, infinity, a BC date, or a seconds-level offset.

items.name: get_decimal
items.sig: fn get_decimal(rows: Rows, r: int, c: int) -> result[decimal.Decimal, str]
items.doc: The exact value of a numeric or integer cell (int2, int4, int8, numeric), at the scale Postgres reports: numeric(12, 2) gives "19.90", not 19.9. err for another column type, NaN or an infinity, or a value past decimal's 38 digits.

items.name: get_int

items.name: get_float
items.sig: fn get_float(rows: Rows, r: int, c: int) -> float
items.doc: float4, float8, numeric, and the integer types. A numeric too precise for a double is rounded; read it with get_text to keep every digit.

items.name: Pool
items.doc: A bounded set of connections to one database, shared by any number of tasks.

items.name: new_pool
items.sig: fn new_pool(url: str, max_open: int) -> result[Pool, str]
items.doc: Parses the url; connects nothing until the first acquire.

items.name: acquire
items.sig: fn acquire(p: Pool, deadline: until) -> result[Conn, str]
items.doc: A connection for the caller's exclusive use, until release(). Prefer pool_query / pool_exec, which cannot forget to release; acquire is for a transaction, which needs several statements on one connection.

items.name: release
items.doc: Returns a connection to the pool: to the oldest waiting task if there is one, else to the idle list. One that is broken, closed, or still inside a transaction is closed instead, and its slot passed on: handing an open transaction to the next caller would run its statements inside someone else's uncommitted work.

items.name: pool_query
items.sig: fn pool_query(p: Pool, sql: str, args: [Arg], deadline: until) -> result[Rows, str]

items.name: pool_exec
items.sig: fn pool_exec(p: Pool, sql: str, deadline: until) -> result[int, str]

items.name: pool_close
items.doc: Closes every idle connection and fails every waiting acquire. Connections in use are closed as they are released; acquire fails from now on.

items.name: Rng
items.doc: A random number generator. Make one with `new` or `from_os`.

items.name: new
items.doc: A generator whose sequence is fixed by `seed`. Every int is a good seed, 0 and -1 included: splitmix64 spreads it over all 256 bits of state.

items.name: from_os
items.doc: A generator seeded from the operating system's CSPRNG, for when runs should differ (load generators, sampling in production). Its outputs are still predictable from earlier ones: this is not a source of secrets.  Read from /dev/urandom (the kernel generator crypto.rand also uses), so importing rand does not link OpenSSL: about 1.3 MB of RSS and 3 ms of start-up that a program using only seeded draws would otherwise pay.

items.name: fork
items.doc: A new generator seeded from `r`, for handing to a spawned task. Seeded parents give seeded children, so a whole run still replays from one seed. `r` advances by one step.

items.name: next_u64
items.doc: The next 64 random bits.

items.name: below
items.sig: fn below(r: Rng, n: int) -> int
items.doc: An int in [0, n), each value equally likely. Panics if n is not positive: there is no int to return, as with an index out of range.

items.name: between
items.sig: fn between(r: Rng, lo: int, hi: int) -> int
items.doc: An int in [lo, hi], both ends included, each value equally likely. Panics if lo > hi. The full range, between(r, MIN, MAX), works.

items.name: unit
items.doc: A float in the unit interval [0, 1): one of 2^53 evenly spaced values, so every float it returns is exact and 1.0 never appears.

items.name: chance
items.sig: fn chance(r: Rng, p: float) -> bool
items.doc: True with probability `p`. p at or below 0 (or NaN) is never, p at or above 1 is always.

items.name: shuffle
items.doc: Reorders `xs` in place, every order equally likely (Fisher-Yates).

items.name: pick
items.doc: One element of `xs`, each equally likely; none if `xs` is empty.

items.name: backoff
items.sig: fn backoff(r: Rng, attempt: int, base: int, cap: int) -> int
items.doc: How long to wait before retry number `attempt` (0 for the first retry): a uniform draw from [0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt)], the "full jitter" strategy. Spreading over the whole interval, not just its top, is what stops a crowd of clients that failed together from retrying together. Units are whatever `base` and `cap` use, nanoseconds for a duration. A negative attempt counts as 0; a base or cap at or below 0 gives 0.

items.name: jitter
items.sig: fn jitter(r: Rng, d: int, frac: float) -> int
items.doc: `d` scaled by a uniform factor in [1 - frac, 1 + frac]: jitter(r, d, 0.1) lands within 10% of d. frac is clamped to [0, 1] (NaN counts as 0), so the result is never negative. A d at or below 0 gives 0.

items.name: normal
items.doc: A standard normal value: mean 0, stddev 1. Scale it for any other: `mu + sigma * rand.normal(r)`. The ziggurat method (Marsaglia and Tsang, 256 layers): about 99% of draws cost one 64-bit step, a table lookup and a multiply, with no log, sqrt or trigonometry.

items.name: exponential
items.doc: An exponential value with rate 1 (mean 1). Divide by a rate for any other: `rand.exponential(r) / rate`. Ziggurat, as normal() is.

items.name: REPLY_SIMPLE
items.doc: The five RESP2 reply types. A reply is always one of exactly one.

items.name: REPLY_BULK
items.sig: let REPLY_BULK = 3; // $len\r\n<bytes> (bulk holds it, none when nil)

items.name: Decoded
items.doc: A decoded reply plus how many bytes of the input it consumed, so a connection holding a read buffer knows what to keep.

items.name: encode
items.doc:
Encode one command invocation as a RESP2 array of bulk strings: SET key value  ->  *3
$3
SET
$3
key
$5
value
 Takes already-encoded argument bytes, so binary-safe values pass through untouched. Pure: no I/O, no allocation beyond the result.

items.name: decode
items.doc: Decode one RESP2 reply from the front of `buf`. ok(none) means the buffer ends mid-message -- feed more bytes and retry. ok(some(d)) consumed d.consumed bytes; anything after them is the next message. err means the bytes violate the protocol: never retry on the same connection.

items.name: decode_at
items.sig: fn decode_at(buf: bytes, pos: int) -> result[opt[Decoded], str]
items.doc: Decode one reply starting at `pos` instead of 0, for readers that keep one long-lived buffer and an offset into it (see Conn): no slicing, so no per-recv copy of everything already buffered. consumed counts from `pos`.

items.name: slot
items.doc: The hash slot of a key, 0..16383. `{...}` hash tags force colocation: only what sits between the first `{` and the next `}` is hashed. Empty tags hash the whole key, and a `{` with no `}` is literal.

items.name: parse_url
items.doc: Parse redis://[[username:]password@]host[:port][/db][?sslmode=...]. rediss:// forces sslmode=require. Percent-escapes in credentials and database decode the same way pg's URLs do.

items.name: Conn
items.doc: One server connection: exactly one round trip in flight at a time, serialized by lock. A Conn is safe to share between tasks; every public call below takes the lock for its whole exchange.

items.name: connect_config
items.sig: fn connect_config(cfg: Config, deadline: until) -> result[Conn, str]
items.doc: Open a connection from a parsed Config and run the handshake (AUTH when a password is set, SELECT when db is not 0). The deadline covers everything: DNS, TCP connect, TLS upgrade, login.

items.name: connect
items.sig: fn connect(url: str, deadline: until) -> result[Conn, str]
items.doc: Open a connection from a URL. See parse_url for the shape.

items.name: do
items.sig: fn do(c: Conn, args: [bytes], deadline: until) -> result[Reply, str]
items.doc: Run one command: args[0] is the command name. Exactly one reply is consumed, so at most one command is ever in flight per Conn; hold no lock of your own -- this takes c.lock for the round trip. Refused inside MULTI: queued commands answer +QUEUED, which no typed shape could read -- use queue there.

items.name: close
items.doc: Shut the connection down. In-flight calls on other tasks finish (or hit their own deadlines) first; close waits for the lock.

items.name: usable
items.doc: True while commands may still be attempted: not closed, not broken. A server-side idle close is discovered on use, which marks the connection broken then.

items.name: ints
items.doc: Sorts xs in place, ascending. Unstable. Answers an already-sorted or strictly descending list in one scan, and duplicate-heavy data in no more passes than its distinct values take to settle, so the whole call is allocation-free either way.

items.name: floats
items.doc: Same engine over floats, with a total order despite the type's own: NaN values sort before every number and equal to each other (Go's `sort.Float64s` rule), which is what makes the partition finite.

items.name: strings
items.doc: Same engine over strings, bytewise: `""` sorts first, and the order is exactly what `<` gives — bytes, not locale, not Unicode points.

items.name: by
items.sig: fn by[T, K](xs: [T], key: fn(T) -> K) -> [T]
items.doc: Sorts xs in place by key, ascending. Unstable: when two keys are equal, which was first is whatever the comparisons fell into. A call is free to permute equal keys differently on a re-run, so anything whose output must not change between runs uses `by_stable`.

items.name: by_stable
items.sig: fn by_stable[T, K](xs: [T], key: fn(T) -> K) -> [T]
items.doc: Sorts xs in place by key, ascending, and equal keys keep their original order: an adaptive merge sort. Natural runs are kept (a strictly descending run is reversed, which keeps order for equal keys, since a strictly descending run has none), windows of 32 are insertion-sorted, and runs merge bottom-up taking the left on equal keys. Nearly-sorted data therefore costs about one comparison per element, not n log n.

items.name: search_ints
items.doc: The first index of v in xs, sorted ascending, or none. On a list which is not sorted the result is defined but useless; it never reads past the list.

items.name: search_floats
items.doc: Same contract over floats: that includes searching for NaN, which finds the first NaN and sorts first under sort.floats. The index found for a searched NaN is where the first NaN of the list sits.

items.name: search_strings
items.doc: Same contract over strings: the first index of an exactly equal string, bytewise as `sort.strings` orders them.

items.name: search_by
items.sig: fn search_by[T, K](xs: [T], key: fn(T) -> K, v: K) -> opt[int]
items.doc: Lower bound over a list already sorted by key: the first index whose key is not before v. Equality is `!(a < b) && !(b < a)`, which is `==` for int and str keys; for a float key it reads equal NaNs -- both raw comparisons false -- as a hit, the same reading `by` gives them.

items.name: parse_rfc3339

"t" and "z" and a space for "T" are accepted, as RFC 3339 allows. A missing offset is refused: a timestamp without one names no instant.

items.name: parse_http_date
items.doc: An HTTP date. RFC 9110 has recipients accept three forms, and so does this:  Tue, 13 Oct 2026 09:30:15 GMT       IMF-fixdate (what everything sends) Tuesday, 13-Oct-26 09:30:15 GMT     RFC 850 (two-digit year: more than 50 years ahead means last century) Tue Oct 13 09:30:15 2026            asctime

items.name: Interval
items.doc: A half-open span [start, end): it contains its start, not its end, so back-to-back intervals (09:00-10:00, 10:00-11:00) do not overlap.

items.name: Interval.length

items.name: Cron
items.doc: A five-field cron schedule: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week. Each field takes `*`, numbers, ranges (`9-17`), lists (`1,15`), steps (`*/15`, `0-30/10`), month names (JAN-DEC) and weekday names (SUN-SAT; 0 and 7 are both Sunday). Macros: @yearly @annually @monthly @weekly @daily @midnight @hourly. As in Vixie cron, when both day fields are restricted a day matches either one.

items.name: Cron.next_after
items.sig: fn next_after(self: Cron, t: Time, z: Zone) -> opt[Time]
items.doc: The first run strictly after `t`, read on the clocks of `z`; none when the schedule never matches (Feb 30) within eight years. A run whose wall time a daylight-saving change skips happens when the clock reaches it (moved forward); one the change repeats runs once.

items.name: DAY

items.name: IsoWeek

items.name: ZonedTime.add_months

items.name: NIL
items.doc: The nil and max UUIDs (RFC 9562 sections 5.9 and 5.10).

items.name: v4
items.doc: A random UUID, version 4: 122 random bits.

items.name: v7
items.doc: A time-ordered UUID, version 7, stamped with the current wall-clock time: 48 bits of unix milliseconds, then 74 random bits.

items.name: v7_at
items.doc: A version 7 UUID stamped with `unix_ms` instead of the clock: for tests, and for ids that must carry an event's own time. Errors if `unix_ms` is negative or does not fit in 48 bits.

items.name: is_valid
items.doc: Is `s` a UUID in canonical form: 36 characters, lowercase hex digits, hyphens at 8, 13, 18 and 23? Any version and variant passes, so ids made elsewhere (Postgres's gen_random_uuid, another service) are accepted. Upper case, braces and urn:uuid: are not: run those through `parse`.

items.name: parse
items.doc: The canonical form of a UUID written any common way: canonical, upper or mixed case, in braces ({...}), as a urn:uuid: URN, or as 32 hex digits without hyphens. The error names the position and what was expected there.

items.name: version
items.doc: The version number of a canonical UUID (4 for v4, 7 for v7, 0 for NIL), or none if `s` is not canonical.

items.name: time_ms
items.doc: When a v7 UUID was made, in unix milliseconds. none if `s` is not a canonical version 7 UUID with the RFC 9562 variant: other versions keep no time, or keep it in another layout.

items.name: to_binary
items.doc: The 16 bytes of a UUID, most significant first: the binary form databases store (Postgres `uuid` on the wire, a BINARY(16) column). Accepts every spelling `parse` does.

items.name: from_binary
items.doc: The canonical form of 16 bytes, the reverse of `to_binary`.

items.name: options
items.doc: The defaults: no extra headers or subprotocols, 32 MiB messages, no compression, no keepalive pings.

items.name: dial
items.sig: fn dial(url: str, deadline: until) -> result[Conn, str]
items.doc: Connect to url (ws:// or wss://) with the default options.

items.name: dial_with
items.sig: fn dial_with(url: str, o: Options, deadline: until) -> result[Conn, str]
items.doc: Connect, send the opening handshake, and check the server's answer.

items.name: send_text
items.sig: fn send_text(c: Conn, text: str, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
items.doc: Send a text message.

items.name: send_text_bytes
items.sig: fn send_text_bytes(c: Conn, data: bytes, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
items.doc: Send a text message given as bytes, checked to be UTF-8 first: for text holding U+0000, which a str cannot (it ends at the first zero byte), and for text already in a byte buffer.

items.name: send_binary
items.sig: fn send_binary(c: Conn, data: bytes, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
items.doc: Send a binary message.

items.name: ping
items.sig: fn ping(c: Conn, payload: bytes, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
items.doc: Send a ping (payload up to 125 bytes); the server's pong is consumed by recv. options().ping_every sends them on a schedule instead.

items.name: recv
items.sig: fn recv(c: Conn, deadline: until) -> result[opt[Message], str]
items.doc: The next message, or none when the deadline passes first (nothing is lost: a later call carries on). Pings are answered and pongs consumed on the way. A Close message means the server ended the connection; the handshake is answered and the next call is an error.

items.name: text
items.doc: The text of a text message. A str ends at its first zero byte, so text holding U+0000 is cut there: m.data has every byte.

items.name: close
items.sig: fn close(c: Conn, code: int, reason: str, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
items.doc: The close handshake: send a close frame with code (1000 normal, or 3000-4999 for applications) and a reason of at most 123 bytes, then wait for the server's close (until deadline) and close the socket. If another task is in recv, that task sees the server's answer as a Close message and this call returns once the frame is sent.

items.name: close_now
items.doc: Close the socket now, with no close handshake: for a connection that is already broken or must stop at once.

items.name: is_open
items.doc: Whether the connection is open (not closing or closed).

items.name: reason
items.doc: Why the connection ended, or "" while it is open.

items.name: Cert
items.doc: One certificate, as parsed. `der` is exactly the bytes it came from, so a chain can be passed back to verify or stored without re-encoding.

items.name: Verify
items.doc: What verify checks besides the signatures and the chain to a root.

items.name: Request
items.doc: The names a CSR or self-signed certificate is for.

items.name: parse_pem
items.doc: Every CERTIFICATE block of a PEM text, in order. Other blocks and text between them are skipped; a block that does not decode is an error.

items.name: parse_der
items.doc: One DER certificate, or several concatenated (as a TLS chain and net.tls_peer_certs give them).

items.name: matches_host
items.sig: fn matches_host(c: Cert, host: str) -> bool
items.doc: Does the certificate name `host`? RFC 6125: subjectAltName entries only, never the subject CN; a wildcard only as the whole left-most label, for exactly one label ("*.example.com" matches "a.example.com", not "example.com" or "a.b.example.com"). An IP literal matches IP entries.

items.name: valid_at
items.sig: fn valid_at(c: Cert, unix: int) -> bool
items.doc: Is `unix` (seconds) inside the certificate's validity period?

items.name: expires_in
items.doc: Seconds until the certificate expires; negative once it has.

items.name: verify
items.sig: fn verify(chain: [Cert], v: Verify) -> result[bool, str]
items.doc: Checks `chain` (the leaf first, then any intermediates) up to one of the roots: every signature, validity at `v.at`, and the host and purpose when set. ok(true), or why not, in words that do not change with the OpenSSL version: "x509: certificate has expired", "x509: certificate is not yet valid", "x509: hostname mismatch", "x509: IP address mismatch", "x509: certificate is not for this purpose", "x509: certificate signed by unknown authority", "x509: self-signed certificate not in the roots", "x509: certificate signature does not verify", "x509: issuer is not a CA", "x509: path length constraint exceeded"; rarer failures carry OpenSSL's own reason.

items.name: csr
items.sig: fn csr(key_pem: str, r: Request) -> result[str, str]
items.doc: A certificate signing request (PKCS#10, PEM) for `r`'s names, signed with `key_pem` (an RSA, EC or Ed25519 private key in PEM). It is what an ACME server, or any CA, is sent: it carries the names and the public key, and proves the sender holds the private key.

items.name: self_signed
items.sig: fn self_signed(key_pem: str, r: Request, days: int) -> result[str, str]
items.doc: A certificate for `r`'s names, signed by its own key and valid from now for `days` (1 to 36500): for development TLS and tests. It is a leaf (not a CA) for server and client auth; to verify it, pass its own PEM as `roots_pem`.
